## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.64108.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.64108.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

The reviewers are satisfied with the thought and effort the authors put into this revised manuscript and are now happy to publish this interesting study without reservation. In this emerging model organism for neuroscience, the authors nicely demonstrate with calcium imaging and loss-of-function approaches, the identification of diverse sensorimotor activity patterns to mechanical stimulation, driven by unique networks of neurons.

Decision letter after peer review:

[Editors’ note: the authors submitted for reconsideration following the decision after peer review. What follows is the decision letter after the first round of review.]

Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Multiple nerve rings coordinate Hydra mechanosensory behavior" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

We are sorry to say that, after consultation with the reviewers, we have decided that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife.

Specifically, all of the reviewers agreed that the emerging Hydra system holds great promise for neuroscience discoveries. Moreover, some of the findings presented here have the potential to be of use to other scientists who work in this system. However, we felt that the findings here were too preliminary and underdeveloped to warrant publication in eLife in its current form. In particular reviewers felt that (1) multiple locations across the Hydra's body should be stimulated coupled with mapping the behavioral and neuronal correlates of such stimulation, (2) the pan-neuronal nature of the bulk calcium measurements made it challenging to fully appreciate which neuronal circuits might be driving the sensorimotor responses, (3) uniform proxies for measuring/plotting the behavior would be useful, (4) the ablation studies lacked cellular resolution, similar to the calcium imaging experiments. Below, please find detailed comments that we hope will help to strengthen this work for submission elsewhere.

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript by Badhiwala et al., is an interesting study using the emerging model system Hydra, which has many advantages for studying the entire nervous system of an animal during simple behavior. Some of the foundational neuroscience papers in this field have only come out in the past few years, and new studies such as the one here, have the potential to contribute to an important early literature. Despite clear reasons for enthusiasm, there are a few issues in this work that require attention prior to publication. Although I appreciate building the microfluidic device with simultaneous pan-neuronal imaging, the nature of the new biological insights provided here are somewhat limited. The preliminary nature of some experiments also make it challenging to judge the potential implications of the work.

1. The pressurized stimulation of the hydra appeared to be specific to the center of the body. The authors don't mention why this region was chosen, which seems critical to this study. Relatedly, it appears important to test multiple areas across the hydra with this system. Might we expect to see different sensorimotor behaviors, and thus different neural outputs?

2. The authors reference a recent single cell study characterizing multiple neuronal cell types in hydra. This work would greatly benefit by using some cell-type resolution studies to determine the functional nature of the neurons being activated as opposed to solely using pan-neuronal GCAMP imaging. It appears that since they can put GCAMP in all neurons, they may be able to also introduce GCaMP into specific subsets of neurons based on cellular identity. This point becomes more salient because a major take-home from this paper is that the spontaneous behavior and firing patterns is nearly identical to the stimulus evoked patterns, except for an apparent increase in firing rate. The true nature of the mechanosensory response might be revealed with cell-type specific experiments.

3. Although the authors reference whole animal imaging, they focus imaging analysis on peduncle and hypostomal nerve rings, despite the videos showing calcium activity in other areas throughout the body. Moreover, are the authors certain their pan-neuronal genetic strategy equally samples neurons throughout the body? In other words, is it possible that the apparent increase in activity in the nerve ring over other areas is being driven by a technical artifact of these neurons being labeled better?

4. While I appreciate the resection studies to get at "loss-of-function" experiments, this is a somewhat blunt hammer approach, and potentially confounds clear interpretation. It is important to establish which neurons are killed and to what extent, and how many, if any began to regenerate throughout this process. The concern is that residual activity from neurons not ablated may be driving this response, especially in light of the authors surprising finding that "footless" animals show that the aboral nerve ring is not required for spontaneous or mechanosensory responses.

Reviewer #2:

The Hydra, in the phylum cnidaria, is a near microscopic freshwater animal that has recently resurfaced as an attractive model organism in neuroscience due to its optically accessible transparent body, sparsely distributed neural network, and simple behaviors. In this manuscript, Badhiwala and colleagues use calcium imaging of the Hydra neural network, combined with surgical resection and microfluidics pressure stimulation to identify body regions indispensable for mechanosensory activity. They report that while resection of the aboral region did not abolish the mechanical response, resection of the oral region attenuated this response, while combined resection of oral and aboral regions showed the greatest effect. They also find a correlation between reduced stimulated activity and spontaneous activity, suggesting a common mechanism that gives rise to both activities. While this study takes on an innovative approach by using a microfluidics device to mechanically stimulate the hydra under optical recording there are a number of conceptual and technical limitations. Perhaps my biggest concern is that despite the potential, the data are rather low resolution (body transections and bulk calcium responses) and as such the conclusions supported by the provided data do not significantly extend our current knowledge.

1. The authors have designed a microfluidic device that allows them to simultaneously mechanically stimulate, monitor movement and functionally image a hydra. The highly quantifiable nature of the microfluidic device a great asset, although this potential is not deeply explored. While I can see how the microfluidic stimulation could offer benefits over fluid jet or blunt probe, more in-depth characterization is needed.

2. What is the spatial distribution of the pressure pulse stimulus on the Hydra body? How far does the mechanical force spread from the region directly touching the pressure valve?

3. The use of the microfluidic device was limited. Have the authors attempted to map mechanical sensitivity across the Hydra body by stimulating different sites?

4. The authors spatially average a population response from a large region of interest as compared to recording calcium responses from single neurons. This should be specifically stated in the Results section. More importantly, to provide insight into network function much smaller ROIs over multiple sites are needed instead of the bulk activity of the entire peduncle. This analysis would allow the authors to significantly extend the findings from this work, as the lure of the optically clear and small hydra is that neural representation and coding can be tracked over large portions of the network at cellular resolution.

5. It is unclear where the recorded signals are coming from and if movement is creating artifacts. Have authors corrected for movement? The supplemental movies show a stationary region of interest and moving animal, in some cases parts of animal moving in and out. Furthermore, please explain how the background is subtracted. There is a large fluorescent signal coming from of the entire body/ middle columnar part of the body and spontaneous firing that makes interpretation of the data difficult.

6. Contraction is a behavioral response of the animal; however, the authors use 'contraction' do describe calcium imaging responses throughout the figures and text. This should be avoided.

7. The authors may wish to rephrase the wording of the paper title. I do not think this work establishes definitively that "multiple nerve rings" are important for coordinating mechanosensory behavior.

8. Furthermore, the claim that the observed "linear relationship" between the spontaneous contraction probability and resection type is evidence for shared neural pathways is not strongly supported by the provided data. These data are fairly coarse resolution and include only 3 animals in each group with highly variable responses (Figure 4C). Additionally, they do not provide evidence to distinguish the motor circuits they hypothesized these neural nets converge upon.

Reviewer #3:

The authors probe mechanosensory processing in Hydra by measuring calcium activity in neurons and muscles in response to precise mechanosensory stimulation in whole and resected animals. The authors' claims are well supported by the evidence. The development of a mechanosensory delivery system for Hydra is also a significant methodological advancement. Taken together, the work advances our understanding of the Hydra nervous system and is a needed step towards developing Hydra as a powerful model for systems neuroscience.

1) One issue is that different measures of "mechanosensory response" are used at different places in the manuscript. In some contexts, a response is defined as calcium activity in neurons (Figure 2), and elsewhere as calcium activity in muscles (Figure 3 and 4). And in Figure 2 SuppFig2 muscle contractions are also measured using MeKs. The relation between neural activity, muscle activity and body movement is, of course, of high interest, and the paper explores this. But, if technically possible, it would be helpful to report a single metric of behavior that could be used in all experiments. For example, it might be possible to use video of the animal's pose or body length to measure contractions in all experiments. At a minimum the reasoning behind choice of measurement of response for each experiment could be discussed explicitly.

2) Related: Without a consistent measure of behavior, it will be important to further clarify figures so that a reader can tell at-a-glance how contraction probability is being measured.

results.result: Hydra vulgaris is characterized as an emerging model organism for neuroscience with a diffuse nervous system composed of endodermal and ectodermal networks, featuring nerve rings in oral (hypostomal) and aboral (peduncle) regions with distinct neuronal cell types and lower turnover rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5-C12 collectively establish Hydra's anatomical and molecular characteristics as a model organism. The claims are well-supported by citations to prior work (C5, C6, C7, C12), anatomical descriptions (C8, C9), and single-cell RNA sequencing data (C10, C11, C12) shown in Figure 1. These foundational claims provide context for the experimental work.

results.result: The microfluidic mechanical stimulation system delivers localized force with most mechanical displacement concentrated within ~250 µm of the valve center, with negligible displacement beyond 750 µm.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by quantitative tracking of 222 neurons during stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The measurements show spatial distribution of mechanical force with statistical confidence intervals (95% CI), demonstrating the locality of the stimulus. This technical validation is essential for interpreting subsequent mechanosensory experiments.

results.result: Mechanical stimulation generates calcium signals in neurons throughout the body, with striking co-activation of peduncle nerve ring neurons appearing as single spikes (contraction pulses) or volleys (contraction bursts), and the peduncle ROI faithfully represents individual neuron activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C18 describe the basic neural response to mechanical stimulation, supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 2b, Videos 2-3, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The validation that large ROI measurements correlate with individual neuron tracking (C17-C18) is important for justifying the analysis approach used throughout the study.

results.result: Hydra's mechanosensory response probability depends on stimulus intensity, with strong stimuli (20-25 psi) producing 5× higher response probability than spontaneous activity, while weak stimuli (5 psi) produce no response. Strong stimulation increases single-pulse contractions and entrains contraction frequency to match the 31 s inter-stimulus interval.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24, C66 establish the stimulus-response relationship with quantitative data from N=3 animals per condition (Figure 2e-h). Statistical comparisons are provided with means, SEMs, and significance values. The psychometric function and temporal patterning changes are well-documented, though the sample size is modest (N=3 per condition).

results.result: The aboral end of Hydra shows lower mechanosensory sensitivity than the mid-body region (response probability 0.1 vs 0.42), independent of animal size, though the same motor program is initiated regardless of stimulation location.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 demonstrate regional differences in mechanosensitivity supported by experiments at different body locations (Figure 2—figure supplement 7). The control for animal size (C26) addresses a potential confound. However, the claim about the "same motor program" (C27) is somewhat qualitative and based on observation rather than detailed quantification.

results.result: The mechanosensory response is mediated by electrically coupled cells rather than passive calcium diffusion, as evidenced by fast response times (~0.5 s) that are inconsistent with theoretical diffusion times (~100 s) and fast propagation of calcium activity throughout the endoderm.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 present a mechanistic argument supported by response time measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 8) and theoretical calculations. The comparison between observed response times (0.1-0.6 s) and calculated diffusion times (~100 s) provides strong evidence against passive diffusion. Citation to aneural Hydra studies (C30) provides additional support.

results.result: The 6-12 hr recovery period after resection allows wound closure and initial regeneration events but is insufficient for neuronal regeneration (which requires 30-72 hr), as confirmed by qPCR showing loss of specific neuronal cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 establish the experimental timeline for resection studies with supporting citations and qPCR validation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1-2). The qPCR data directly confirms loss of specific neuronal subtypes, addressing a critical control for the resection experiments. The timeline is well-justified by prior literature.

results.result: The aboral peduncle nerve ring is not required for mechanosensory responses or spontaneous contractions, as footless animals show similar response magnitudes and probabilities to whole animals despite removal of this highly active neural network.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39, C70 present a surprising finding supported by quantitative comparisons between footless and whole animals (N=8 for 20 min stimulation, N=3 for 60 min; Figure 3b-c, Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Statistical analysis includes effect sizes (Cohen's d, Cliff's delta) and p-values. This challenges the expected role of the peduncle network based on its correlation with contractions.

results.result: Removal of the oral hypostome and tentacles (headless Hydra) significantly reduces both mechanosensory response probability (>2× lower) and spontaneous contraction probability (>3× lower) compared to whole animals, though responses remain significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 demonstrate the importance of the oral network with quantitative data (N=8 for 20 min, N=3 for 60 min; Figure 3b-c, Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Statistical comparisons show significant reductions with effect sizes. The finding that headless animals retain some response capability is important for understanding network organization.

results.result: Longitudinally bisected animals (removing ~50% of tissue while preserving oral and aboral neuronal subtypes) show intermediate responses between whole and headless animals, demonstrating that the reduced response in headless animals depends on specific neuronal types removed rather than injury per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 provide an important control for the resection experiments (N=8 for 20 min, N=3 for 60 min; Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The comparison between bisected and headless animals (C44-C45) addresses the alternative explanation that tissue damage causes reduced responses. The inference about network integrity (C47) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Body column animals lacking both oral and aboral nerve rings show the most dramatically reduced mechanosensory responses, with the lowest magnitude increase upon stimulation despite showing significant increases compared to spontaneous activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52, C68 demonstrate the cumulative effect of removing both regional networks (N=6 for 20 min, N=3 for 60 min; Figure 3b-c, Figure 3—figure supplement 3-4). The control showing no temporal increase in non-stimulated animals (C51, Figure 3—figure supplement 4) is important for ruling out time-dependent effects. Statistical analysis includes effect sizes.

results.result: Mechanosensory and spontaneous behaviors are regulated by neural ensembles localized to oral and aboral regions that work together in compensatory roles, with sufficient functional redundancy that removal of one region is tolerated, while the body column retains minimal processing capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61, C67, C69, C77-C78 synthesize the resection experiments into a model of network organization. The conclusions are well-supported by the pattern of results across different resection conditions. However, these are higher-level interpretations that involve inference beyond the direct measurements. The concept of "compensatory roles" (C69) is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: At least two independent neuronal networks mediate mechanosensory responses: contraction burst (CB) neurons showing fast responses (<1 s) throughout the body, and mechanically responsive (MR) neurons in the oral region showing slower responses (~10 s after stimulation) without spontaneous activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59, C63-C64, C79 identify distinct neuronal networks through single-neuron tracking and correlation analysis (N=3 Hydra; Figure 4). The temporal differences between CB and MR neurons are clear in the data. The identification is based on correlation analysis and stimulus-aligned activity patterns. However, the sample size is small (N=3) and the number of tracked neurons per animal is limited.

results.result: Localized touch produces increased calcium activity in both peduncle neurons and endodermal epitheliomuscular cells, associated with body contractions.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 summarizes the basic observation supported by calcium imaging in both neuronal (Figure 2) and muscle (Figure 3) transgenic lines, with validation from simultaneous electrophysiology (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). This is a well-established finding that integrates multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: MR neurons may consist of ec4 neurons, the only neuronal subtype in the oral end with unknown function.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is explicitly speculative ("It is possible that...") and based only on anatomical location matching between MR neurons and ec4 neurons. No direct evidence (e.g., cell-type-specific markers, genetic manipulation) is provided to test this hypothesis. This remains an interesting but unvalidated speculation.

results.result: The peduncle nerve ring may coordinate body contractions by enhancing neural signals to epithelial cells and may function as motor neurons, supported by calcium propagation from foot to hypostome and reduced contraction duration in body column animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 propose functional roles for the peduncle network. While C72 provides some supporting data (4 s reduction in contraction duration; Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and C73 cites prior work on calcium propagation, claims C71 and C74 are explicitly speculative. The evidence is suggestive but indirect, and alternative explanations are not ruled out.

results.result: A proposed model suggests the hypostome serves as an integration point where sensory and motor information converge, with information then communicated to the peduncle for amplification and coordinated whole-body control.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 present a conceptual model based on the experimental findings. While the model is consistent with the data (oral region importance, peduncle correlation with contractions), it involves significant inference beyond direct measurements. The model is explicitly presented as a proposal ("we propose") and lacks direct evidence for information flow pathways or the specific roles of "integration" and "amplification."
